articles.title: The 20% of Tasks I Deliberately Do Not Give the Agent
articles.excerpt: Every honest account of running an agent eventually has to say what it does not hand over. Mine is about a fifth of the work, and the reasons cluster into four kinds. The agent is good at tasks where…
articles.body: Every honest account of running an agent eventually has to say what it does not hand over. Mine is about a fifth of the work, and the reasons cluster into four kinds. 1. Anything where being wrong is expensive and silent The agent is good at tasks where a mistake shows up immediately: a broken build, a failed test, a page that does not load. It is bad at tasks where a mistake looks like success. An example from my own week: renaming a column in a schema. The migration runs, the app starts, everything is green, and one report has been quietly wrong since Tuesday. Nothing in the run said anything was wrong, because from the agent's point of view nothing was. I still do those tasks, I just do them with the agent watching me rather than the other way around. 2.

articles.title: The Appearance Design Process Has Six Gates — Not One Pretty Render
articles.excerpt: Start with the verdict. What goes wrong in an appearance design process is rarely the drawing — it is that nobody agreed where one stage ends. The client believes week three buys a 3D model ready to c…
articles.body: Start with the verdict. What goes wrong in an appearance design process is rarely the drawing — it is that nobody agreed where one stage ends. The client believes week three buys a 3D model ready to cut steel; we are still arguing about proportions in a sketch. After ten years and more than 320 products, I have compressed the process into six delivery gates: requirement definition → concept sketches (2–3 form directions) → 2D renderings and CMF → 3D surface appearance model → appearance prototype validation → appearance freeze and tooling drawing. The first three gates decide what the product looks like. The last three decide whether it can be built and still look like that. The dividing line is not how attractive the rendering is.

articles.title: 🔓 IDOR / BOLA: How to Find the #1 API Vulnerability — and Actually Prove It
articles.excerpt: Broken Object Level Authorization — IDOR, to most of us — is the single most common serious bug in modern APIs. It sits at #1 on the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), and it's the one I watch sail pas…
articles.body: Broken Object Level Authorization — IDOR, to most of us — is the single most common serious bug in modern APIs. It sits at #1 on the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) , and it's the one I watch sail past a scanner, past a code review, and straight into production, where it lives for years. Not because it's clever. Because it's boring : the application carefully checks who you are , and then forgets to check whether the thing you just asked for is actually yours . This guide walks the whole path — what IDOR/BOLA is, how it works, how to find it, and the part most write-ups skip entirely: how to prove it , cleanly, without touching a single real user's data.

articles.title: Cooking Up Magick Book Review
articles.excerpt: Cooking Up Magick Book Review
articles.body: The first book in a new series called The Dell Chronicles, HL Bernabe’s Cooking Up Magick sets out to be a cozier fantasy version of The Lord of the Rings . And in many ways, it does pull directly from J.R.R. Tolkien’s world. The main character, Paisley, is a halfling who gets swept up on an adventure with a pair of dwarves, but unbeknownst to her, there’s also an evil overlord that has just returned after centuries – and she’s the only hope the world has to actually stop him. The similarities to The Hobbit and LOTR pretty much end there though, and you don’t get nearly enough detail in the first book to effectively flesh out this alternate version of Middle-earth. What you do get is a lovable main character who is surrounded by an interesting cast of characters.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 20, 1970: The Soviet Union launches last-ever Zond moon mission
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 20, 1970, the Soviet Union launched the Zond 8 spacecraft on a mission to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 20, 1970, the Soviet Union launched the Zond 8 spacecraft on a mission to the moon. This was the last mission in the Zond program. After the first three Zond missions explored Venus and Mars , the next ones were circumlunar missions that flew around the moon before returning to Earth. Although there was no crew on board, the Zond spacecraft was designed with cosmonauts in mind. The Zond missions served as test flights for the Soviet Union's plans to send cosmonauts to the moon. But those plans for crewed flights never came to fruition. This was partly because the U.S. had already put astronauts on the moon , but also because the Zond missions had a lot of technical problems. Zond 8 was considered a success — even though its guidance system malfunctioned on the way back to Earth.
